claim: RMS Titanic sank at about 02:20 ship's time on 15 April 1912.
Titanic carried 20 lifeboats (16 wooden, 4 collapsible) with room for about 1,178 people.
About 705-712 people survived; Carpathia picked up the survivors (Wikipedia gives 710; other tallies 705-712).

sources.title: House Divided / Dickinson: survivors variously given 705-708

claim: Many lifeboats were launched partly empty: e.g. No. 7 left with about 27-28 people in a boat for 65; No. 2 with 25 of 40.

sources.title: Smithsonian Magazine: Photos of the Titanic tragedy from 101 years ago

qualification: narration says 'many half empty' (approximate, not all boats)

claim: The sea temperature that night was about -2 C (28 F), below freezing for fresh water (sea water freezes lower).

sources.title: Cruise Hive: How cold was the water when the Titanic sank?
Encyclopedia Titanica forum: Temperature of water

qualification: commonly reported figure (28 F); some estimates differ, so narration says 'about minus two degrees'

claim: Sudden immersion in cold water triggers the cold-shock response: an involuntary gasp and hyperventilation in roughly the first minute; a gasp with the head under water can inhale water and drown.

sources.title: Canadian Safe Boating Council: the 1-10-1 principle

claim: The 1-10-1 rule: about 1 minute of cold shock, about 10 minutes of meaningful movement before the muscles of the arms and legs fail, about 1 hour before unconsciousness from hypothermia; the timings vary and are shorter in colder water.

sources.title: Canadian Safe Boating Council: the 1-10-1 principle

qualification: memory aid, not a stopwatch: narration says 'Ten minutes, maybe less'

claim: Lifeboat No. 14, under Fifth Officer Harold Lowe, is described as the only lifeboat to go back to search for survivors after the sinking; it pulled a few people from the water (about four, one of whom died).

sources.title: US Senate Inquiry: testimony of Harold Lowe

qualification: some accounts count Lifeboat 4 (picked up swimmers close by) as a second; narration: 'Only one comes back: Lifeboat fourteen' follows Wikipedia's wording

claim: Charles Joughin, the ship's chief baker, testified that he was in the water for over two hours and survived, holding on to Collapsible B and later taken into another lifeboat.

sources.title: Tim Maltin: Titanic Chief Baker Charles Joughin survived for several hours in the freezing water

qualification: his own account, uncorroborated; historians think his head and upper body stayed out of the water: narration says 'said he lasted about two hours'

claim: Legend says whisky saved Joughin; in his testimony he spoke of a drink of liqueur; scientists say alcohol does not protect against cold water (it can speed heat loss).

sources.title: Tim Maltin: Titanic Chief Baker Charles Joughin survived for several hours in the freezing water

qualification: framed as legend; 'Scientists doubt it helped'

claim: The ship's lights failed shortly before the final plunge (about 2:18 AM), and the hull broke apart between the third and fourth funnels; the stern rose high before sinking.
qualification: picture only (the stern lights flicker out in shot 1)

claim: The night was calm, clear, cold and moonless, with a sky full of stars.
Titanic's fourth (aft) funnel was a dummy used mainly for ventilation.
'Joughin was drunk out of his mind and that is why he survived.'

sources.title: Tim Maltin: Titanic Chief Baker Charles Joughin survived for several hours in the freezing water

qualification: NOT USED: Maltin calls it a myth; Joughin said he was not drunk
